校验和是什么

SHA-256 是一种密码学散列函数：对任意大小的输入（一个文件、一段文本）计算出一个固定 64 个十六进制字符的「指纹」：

e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855

它有三个关键性质：

  • 确定性：同样的输入永远得到同样的输出——所以能当指纹
  • 雪崩效应：改动文件里 1 个字节，指纹面目全非——所以能发现篡改
  • 不可逆与抗碰撞：无法从指纹反推文件，也几乎找不到两个文件同指纹——所以难以伪造

为什么下载要验哈希

  • 下载不完整：大文件传输中断，残缺文件装不上或行为诡异——哈希一验便知
  • 传输被篡改：镜像站、内网代理、被入侵的 CDN 都可能递给你修改过的文件
  • 供应链攻击：软件更新通道被劫持时，官方公布的哈希是最后一道比对标准

做法很简单：发布方公布 文件 + SHA-256 值，你本地对下载的文件算一遍，两边一致才安装。

三平台命令行方法

平台命令
Windows (PowerShell)Get-FileHash 文件名 -Algorithm SHA256
Windows (CMD)certutil -hashfile 文件名 SHA256
macOS / Linuxshasum -a 256 文件名 或 sha256sum 文件名

注意：Windows 的 Get-FileHash 支持 SHA1 / SHA256 / SHA384 / SHA512 / MD5；certutil 的算法名大小写敏感度随版本不同，写 SHA256 最稳。

不想敲命令：本地在线工具

命令行之外的图形化选择：用纯浏览器本地处理的在线校验工具（如 本站 SHA 校验和工具），把文件拖进去就出哈希，再贴上期望值自动比对——文件不上传，与命令行同等安全，对大文件（几 GB 镜像）也适用。

校验失败排查顺序

  1. 算法一致吗：把 SHA-1 的值粘到 SHA-256 框必然不匹配，先核对发布方公布的算法名。
  2. 复制的值干净吗：网页复制常混入空格、换行、大小写差异——本站工具比对时自动忽略，别的工具未必。
  3. 文件完整吗：对比文件大小与发布页标注是否一致；浏览器下载中断常产生截断文件。
  4. 换源重下：以上都排除仍不匹配，说明文件本身有问题——不要安装运行，换官方主源重新下载。

常见问题

Q：哈希和校验和是一回事吗？

A：校验和是泛指，哈希特指 SHA-256 这类密码学散列。日常语境基本同义，但哈希的抗碰撞性远强于旧式求和校验。

Q：SHA-1 和 SHA-256 该用哪个？

A：一律优先 SHA-256；SHA-1 已被实际攻破，只用于兼容旧清单。关键是与发布方公布的算法一致。

Q：Windows 上怎么算 SHA-256？

A：PowerShell 用 Get-FileHash 文件名 -Algorithm SHA256，CMD 用 certutil -hashfile 文件名 SHA256；或用本地在线工具拖文件。

Q：校验和匹配就绝对安全吗？

A：只证明文件与发布方算哈希时的字节一致。官网本身被入侵时哈希也会被替换——重要软件用 GPG 签名做更强验证。

Q：为什么不同工具算出的哈希不一样？

A：最常见是算法不一致，其次是文本被编码转换（CRLF/LF、BOM）后再计算。校验文件永远用文件本体计算。

What a checksum is

SHA-256 is a cryptographic hash function: it maps any input (a file, a text) to a fixed 64-hex-character "fingerprint":

e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855

Three key properties:

  • Deterministic: same input always yields the same output — hence a fingerprint
  • Avalanche effect: flipping 1 byte changes the fingerprint completely — hence tamper detection
  • Irreversible & collision-resistant: can't reverse the fingerprint, and finding two files with one fingerprint is practically impossible — hence hard to forge

Why verify downloads

  • Incomplete downloads: big-file transfers break; a truncated installer fails oddly — a hash check reveals it instantly
  • Tampering in transit: mirrors, internal proxies, or compromised CDNs can hand you modified files
  • Supply-chain attacks: when update channels get hijacked, the officially published hash is the final line of comparison

The workflow is simple: the publisher announces file + SHA-256; you hash your downloaded file locally and install only when the two match.

Command line on three platforms

PlatformCommand
Windows (PowerShell)Get-FileHash filename -Algorithm SHA256
Windows (CMD)certutil -hashfile filename SHA256
macOS / Linuxshasum -a 256 filename or sha256sum filename

Note: Get-FileHash supports SHA1/SHA256/SHA384/SHA512/MD5; certutil algorithm-name casing varies by version — SHA256 is the safe spelling.

No terminal? Local online tools

For a graphical option, use a browser-local checker (like our SHA Checksum tool): drop the file in for an instant digest, paste the expected value for auto-comparison — files are never uploaded, as safe as the command line, and it handles multi-GB images.

Troubleshooting failed checks

  1. Same algorithm? A SHA-1 value never matches a SHA-256 field — check the published algorithm name first.
  2. Clean copy? Web copies often carry spaces, line breaks, and case differences — our tool ignores them; others may not.
  3. File complete? Compare file size with the download page; interrupted browser downloads often truncate.
  4. Re-download from the official source: if all else is ruled out, the file itself is bad — don't install or run it.

FAQ

Q: Are hash and checksum the same thing?

A: "Checksum" is the umbrella term; "hash" specifically means cryptographic digests like SHA-256. In daily use they're interchangeable, but hashes are far stronger than legacy summation checks.

Q: SHA-1 or SHA-256?

A: Prefer SHA-256; SHA-1 is broken and only for legacy manifests. Always match the publisher's published algorithm.

Q: How do I compute SHA-256 on Windows?

A: PowerShell: Get-FileHash filename -Algorithm SHA256; CMD: certutil -hashfile filename SHA256; or drop the file into a local browser tool.

Q: Does a matching checksum mean the file is absolutely safe?

A: It proves your bytes match what the publisher hashed. If the official site itself is breached, the hash is replaced too — use GPG signatures for stronger assurance.

Q: Why do different tools give different hashes?

A: Usually algorithm mismatch; for text, encoding conversion (CRLF/LF, BOM) before hashing. Always hash the file itself.
